followups.q: Does safe static initialization protect later mutation?
followups.a: No. It publishes the initialized state; subsequent mutable updates need their own synchronization.

questions.trap: Assuming class initialization's safety makes every later access to mutable static fields thread-safe.
questions.notes: Connects initialization guarantees with concurrency; exact VM coordination mechanism is not exposed as an API.

questions.question: A service has frequent collections but stable post-GC heap. What would you investigate next?
questions.answer: A stable post-GC live set with frequent collections points more toward allocation churn or insufficient collection headroom than steadily retained objects, though both can coexist. I would measure allocation rate and hot allocation sites, collection frequency and pause or concurrent CPU cost, then correlate them with request throughput and latency. I would compare object survival and promotion trends where the collector reports them. If churn is the driver, reduce avoidable temporary objects or adjust batching after profiling; if the live set grows, investigate roots and owners instead. I would not call this a leak or change heap settings until the metrics establish the dominant cost.

followups.q: Does stable live set mean GC is harmless?
followups.a: No. High churn can still consume CPU and create pauses despite stable occupancy.

followups.q: What would a heap dump add here?
followups.a: It can inspect retained objects, but allocation profiling is usually more direct for churn.

questions.trap: Concluding that frequent collections prove a leak when post-collection occupancy is stable.
questions.notes: Explicitly separates allocation pressure from retention; no incident ownership is claimed.

questions.question: How does Java manage memory: how do objects become unreferenced, and how does garbage collection reclaim them?
questions.answer: An object is eligible for collection when it is unreachable from any GC root, such as thread stacks, static fields and JNI references. You make objects unreachable by letting references go out of scope, nulling them, removing them from the collections that hold them, or holding them only through WeakReference or SoftReference. The heap is generational: new objects start in Eden, survivors move between survivor spaces, and long-lived objects are promoted to the old generation. Minor collections clean the young generation; old-generation work is costlier. G1 is the default collector; ZGC and Shenandoah target very short pauses on large heaps. System.gc() is only a hint, can trigger an expensive full collection and may be disabled, so tune the heap and collector instead of forcing a collection.

followups.q: Can you force garbage collection?
followups.a: No. System.gc() is a request the JVM may ignore, and calling it from application code is generally an anti-pattern.

followups.q: Why can a service run out of memory even though GC runs?
followups.a: Objects that are still reachable, such as an unbounded cache, are never collected.

questions.trap: Saying you can free memory with System.gc(), or that setting a variable to null is always needed.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 4.15 (Morgan Stanley (Synechron), Impetus). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S04-031, JH-S04-036, JH-S04-002.

questions.question: How do you increase a Java application's heap size, and what else counts toward memory in a container?
questions.answer: Set the initial and maximum heap with -Xms and -Xmx, for example java -Xms512m -Xmx4g -jar app.jar; in containers, equal values avoid resizing. In Docker or Kubernetes prefer -XX:MaxRAMPercentage so the JVM derives the heap from the container memory limit, and keep the pod limit above the heap. -Xmx limits only the heap: Metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache, direct buffers and native allocations come on top, which is why a container can be OOM-killed while the heap looks healthy. Raising -Xmx without finding out why memory grows only delays a leak.

followups.q: Why can a pod be killed while heap usage is low?
followups.a: Non-heap memory such as Metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers also counts against the container limit.

followups.q: What should you check before raising -Xmx?
followups.a: Whether memory grows because of a leak or unbounded cache; use GC logs and a heap dump to find out.

questions.trap: Treating -Xmx as the total memory of the process.
questions.notes: Reported in user-provided interview notes, item 4.16 (Accolite). Model answer written for this handbook, not copied from the notes. Related: JH-S14-007, JH-S14-053, JH-S04-048.
